Title: Flaw in Linux NFS file sharing exposes servers to remote takeover
Context: Researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s NFS file-sharing server that lets unauthenticated attackers obtain a root shell on affected systems
Full Text:
Researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s NFS file-sharing server that lets unauthenticated attackers obtain a root shell on affected systems. The flaw remained undetected in the kernel for 12 years, until two researchers, one using an AI agent, discovered it independently.

NFS is typically used inside local networks, including in container networks in Kubernetes clusters and on build servers in development environments. However, it is also enabled on many embedded devices and in network-attached storage (NAS) devices which might be running older kernel versions and can only be patched with firmware updates.

Tracked as CVE-2026-99362 and dubbed NFS2ROOT, the flaw affects systems running the NFSv4.1 or NFSv4.2 versions of the Network File System protocol, the default in many Linux distributions. The vulnerability allows anyone who can reach a server’s port 2049 to corrupt the memory of the nfsd process, the kernel component that serves NFS requests. It is rated 9.8 in severity.

A researcher with French security agency ANSSI, Jérémy Jean, found the bug in August, and his fix was merged into the mainline kernel on September 14.

According to security firm OpenSec Intelligence, which also discovered the heap overflow vulnerability and published technical details about it this week, the flaw can be exploited to gain a shell with root privileges. OpenSec found the bug using its AI-powered security testing harness and submitted its own patch to the Linux kernel maintainers on September 22.

However, since it takes time for all supported kernel branches to backport fixes, the bug wasn’t disclosed, nor was a CVE ID assigned, until November 19.

The flaw was introduced in Linux 3.16 in 2014 and is now patched in eight stable kernel branches: 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2 and 7.4-rc1.

On systems that can’t be immediately patched, administrators are advised to use firewall rules that block access to port 2049 from untrusted systems. Another option is to turn off NFSv4.1 and 4.2 in the nfsd config and then restart the service, but this will turn off pNFS and some features.

Title: Unpatched Cacti zero-day with public PoC gives remote code execution
Context: A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute...
Full Text:
A zero-day vulnerability in the Cacti network monitoring platform has been publicly disclosed, along with a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers.

The exploit, dubbed "4HTTP2SHELL" (previously 4HTTP2ROOT), was published on Thanksgiving Day by a cybersecurity researcher known as ek0ms savi0r from the Church of Malware, who demonstrated how the vulnerability can be exploited using just four HTTP requests.

Cacti is an open-source network monitoring and graphing tool used to monitor the performance of servers, routers, switches, firewalls, and other network infrastructure.

Because the software can store credentials and SNMP passphrases used to access or read data from monitored devices, compromising a Cacti server could potentially give attackers access to other systems on a corporate network.

The researcher published a technical write-up, a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, and a video demonstrating the attack in a GitHub repository named "Sad Girls 0day Club."

"I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests. No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface," explains the researcher.

The vulnerability stems from weak input validation that allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject SQL statements into the application's database and modify commands executed by Cacti's real-time poller.

The attack requires the Cacti guest account to be enabled but does not require attackers to possess valid credentials.

While the researcher demonstrated the exploit providing root access to a vulnerable server, cybersecurity firm watchTowr explains that the privileges gained through exploitation depend on the account running the Cacti web server and poller processes.

In many deployments, this could be a low-privileged web server account rather than root.

Cybersecurity firm RavenAI explains that the attack abuses weak validation of guest users' graph display settings, resulting in a stored SQL injection vulnerability.

The attack involves an attacker saving malicious SQL statements in a guest user's graph display preferences, which are stored in Cacti's database.

When Cacti processes these saved preferences, it executes the SQL statements, allowing the attacker to modify the poller's configuration and cause it to run malicious operating system commands.

The researcher tested the exploit against Cacti Core 1.2.31, but it is unclear whether earlier versions are also vulnerable.

In a separate post on the GitHub repository, ek0ms savi0r expressed frustration with how companies handle vulnerability disclosures, describing years of security reports being dismissed or closed as duplicates, expected behavior, or issues that could not be reproduced.

"Security researchers are not the bad guys. We're the ones trying to help. We're the ones who read the docs, wrote the repro, and sent the packet capture," wrote the researcher.

"We get cracked because we get gaslit for years by billion dollar companies that treat disclosure like a PR problem."

In an Instagram post announcing the Cacti exploit, the researcher shared a video demonstration of the PoC and said that the vulnerability was not reported to Cacti before being released.

Until a patch is released, administrators are advised to deactivate the Cacti guest account and restrict access to the application's web interface to trusted networks.

Administrators should also review poller configurations for unexpected commands and examine application logs for warnings involving non-numeric values in graph display settings, which could indicate attempted exploitation.

As of November 27, there have been no reports of the vulnerability being exploited in attacks.

In this article

A hijacked website can expose your personal data or serve phishing pages and malicious downloads

Attackers are exploiting two critical Drupal flaws to take over websites

Drupal site owners should install the latest security update and check for signs of a break-in

Attackers are exploiting a second critical flaw in Drupal, the content management system (CMS) behind many government, university, corporate, and media websites. Site owners are responsible for applying the fix. For visitors, a hijacked site can put personal data and devices at risk.

On November 18, Drupal released a patch for a remote code execution (RCE) flaw, CVE-2026-132165. The flaw could let attackers take over a site by abusing Drupal’s installer file, install.php. Drupal’s security team received a report of attacks on live sites as early as November 19.

On November 25, Drupal released a second advisory for CVE-2026-136716. Some sites in “unusual or incomplete install states” remained vulnerable to takeover after the first fix, including live sites. Drupal says the new flaw is also being exploited in the wild.

These flaws is a serious problem for website owners, because:

No login is needed. Anonymous attackers can exploit the first flaw. They can attempt to reinstall Drupal and gain control of the site or run code on the server.

Hard to spot. Drupal says the user interface doesn’t show whether a site is in the vulnerable state. Already-compromised sites may no longer show as vulnerable.

Already exploited. CISA added the first flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies until November 27 to fix it.

Drupal has a history of abuse. CISA has flagged six Drupal flaws as exploited since November 2021. Two of them were used in ransomware attacks.

How to stay safe

A hijacked site could expose data stored there, such as account details, email addresses, and form submissions. Attackers could also serve phishing pages or malicious downloads from a trusted domain or deface the site.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

TRY IT NOW

If you’re a visitor or customer:

Be wary of unexpected login prompts, “verify your account” pop-ups, or surprise downloads on sites you normally trust.

Use unique passwords and a password manager. If a site you use reports a breach, change that password and anywhere you reused it.

Turn on multi-factor authentication where it’s offered.

Keep your operating system, browser, and security software up to date.

Treat emails that cite a “security incident” with caution. Go to the site directly instead of clicking links.

If you run a Drupal site:

Update to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14, then run update.php. Drupal says an update hook must run to fix existing production sites.

Block access to /core/install.php in your web server configuration or .htaccess file if you can’t upgrade right away.

Check your logs for unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account (the first account created when a site is installed). Make sure you control the email address on that account, and consider resetting its password.

If you suspect a break-in, follow Drupal’s guide to responding to a hacked site.

Drupal 10.5 and earlier 10.x releases, and Drupal 11.2 and earlier 11.x releases, have reached end of life. Move to a supported release to receive security fixes.

Sites protected by the paid Drupal Steward service are covered against known attack vectors, but Drupal still recommends upgrading.

Patching alone may not be enough. A compromised site can still look normal after patching, so site owners should update Drupal and check for signs of a break-in.

Title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability

CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Drupal warns of new site takeover flaw exploited in attacks
Context: The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites
Full Text:
The Drupal security team says attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that lets them breach and hijack unpatched websites.

Last week, Drupal patched a remote code execution (RCE) flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165 / Fail2Install) that lets anonymous users take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.

While the security issue wasn't initially flagged as being abused in the wild, an update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting it one day after patches were released.

The new security issue (CVE-2026-136716), patched one week later, addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched and also lets attackers hijack vulnerable Drupal sites.

"However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state," Drupal said on Wednesday.

"This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised."

While it has yet to share further details regarding these attacks, Drupal warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised admins to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, and to consider resetting it.

They should also check site logs for unauthorized access, focusing on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account, and follow this guide if they find evidence the site may have been compromised.

Those who can't immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14 should secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been exploited in ransomware attacks.

Title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges
Context: ​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
Full Text:
​A 12-year-old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Network File System (NFS) server, tracked as CVE-2026-99362, allows remote attackers to gain root privileges.

Found by ANSSI's Jérémy Jean (who submitted a fix in August), the flaw has been dubbed NFS2ROOT by cybersecurity firm OpenSec, which shared a full remote-root exploit and a patch with the NFSD maintainers in late September.

The vulnerability has existed since Linux kernel version 3.16 (released in March 2014), and it stems from a heap buffer overflow weakness in the Linux NFS server (nfsd).

NFS2ROOT affects systems with a Linux kernel older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4-rc1 if nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and running and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet.

Successful exploitation lets remote threat actors without privileges corrupt kernel memory and gain root access to vulnerable Linux servers exposed online through low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction.

In NFS2ROOT attacks, the threat actors can exploit this flaw by sending maliciously crafted requests that cause the NFS server to write data beyond an allocated memory buffer. This lets them read kernel memory, bypass KASLR (which protects kernel memory addresses), and place a callback that can execute a command in a released memory area.

When the attacker closes the NFS connection, the kernel executes the embedded command with root privileges, allowing the attacker to gain root control of the unpatched Linux server.

​Although there are no reports of CVE-2026-99362 exploitation in the wild, security teams should apply the latest kernel security updates from their Linux distribution vendor immediately to block potential attacks, then reboot the system to ensure the patched kernel is in use.

Those who can't apply a patch immediately should restrict access to the NFS server over TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or networks. Additionally, if NFS sharing is not required on the system, admins can stop and disable the nfs-server service in /etc/nfs.conf.

"Port 2049 sits open on file servers, NAS appliances, build farms and Kubernetes storage nodes. Since 2014, the Linux kernel listening on it has let anyone who can reach it write into kernel memory before logging in," OpenSec said. "Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow. Patch every host."

While the NFS2ROOT attacks have no network signatures, security teams can still monitor for potential signs of exploitation attempts by checking for kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers on a file server, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions from one source, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_*, svc_* or call_usermodehelper* frames, according to OpenSec.

NFS2ROOT is the latest in a long series of Linux privilege escalation security flaws disclosed and patched since the start of the year, including RefluXFS, CIFSwitch, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, PinTheft, Copy Fail, Pack2TheRoot, and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC.

Title: Unpatched Cacti Zero-Day Enables RCE in Just Four HTTP Requests via Guest Access
Context: Details have emerged about a new zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution
Full Text:
Details have emerged about a new zero-day vulnerability in Cacti, an open-source network monitoring tool, that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution.

The proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, which has yet to be assigned a CVE identifier, has been tracked as 4HTTP2SHELL and 4HTTP2ROOT.

"I found a path from a fresh, unauthenticated HTTP session to command execution as the Cacti server user in four requests," a security researcher who goes by the online alias "ek0ms savi0r" said. "No login. No valid API key. No phishing. Just four HTTP requests against the default guest surface."

The shortcoming affects Cacti Core 1.2.31, the latest version, when the guest account is enabled. It's worth noting that the guest account is disabled by default starting with Cacti version 0.8.7.

At a high level, the vulnerability allows an attacker to abuse the guest access to write an unvalidated value (i.e., non-numeric text) into a setting called "preview_graphs_per_page" via "auth_profile.php?action=update_data." The configuration parameter controls how many graphs are displayed per page when viewing graphs in Preview Mode.

The crafted value takes the form of arbitrary SQL strings that can be turned into a second-order SQL injection by taking advantage of the fact that Cacti does not validate that the user-provided input is actually an integer value. This, in turn, opens the door for arbitrary SQL query execution when the graph preview page ("graph_view.php") is loaded with default filters.

The SQL query demonstrated by "ek0ms savi0r" is an UPDATE statement to modify a record in Cacti's poller table. In the final stage of the attack, the realtime poller endpoint ("graph_realtime.php") is invoked from the same guest session, which causes the modified row from the poller table to be read and passed as input to PHP's popen() function without any allowlist or sanitization checks.

The researcher has pointed out four failures that ultimately make it possible to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution -

The guest can write a numeric setting as an arbitrary string

The stored default bypasses request validation

Cacti's PHP PDO database driver accepts stacked statements through the SQL LIMIT clause

The poller executes a database-stored command string

Successful exploitation of the flaw can allow an attacker to compromise the Cacti server and provide a pivot point to the target network as it exposes sensitive data, or even suppress alerts by modifying the poller table.

"Because Cacti often stores credentials and connection details for routers, switches, servers, and other devices across a network, an attacker who reaches this level of command execution can gain a foothold reaching far beyond the monitoring server itself," watchTowr said in an advisory.

In the absence of a fix, users are advised to disable the guest account and restrict access to the Cacti web interface to mitigate potential risks. It's also essential to review poller configuration entries for unexpected command values and apply the fixes as soon as they become available.

Title: Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug
Context: ” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to...
Full Text: India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens. The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants. DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities. India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.” eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem. While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities. Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®

Title: OpenAI warns GPT-6.2 Astra will hit usage limits 40% faster because it fixed a bug
Context: Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss
Full Text:
OpenAI confirmed that it fixed a 'bug' that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 usage, which means you'll now hit GPT usage limits 40% faster than before.

In a post on X, Tibo Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, admitted to a billing mistake that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most users.

OpenAI says it has fixed the issue but warned that the same tasks will now consume more of users' allowances.

"We've fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your plan's usage allowance," Sottiaux explained.

"Comparing to last week, you will reach your limits 40% faster on GPT-6.2 Astra and 25% faster on Sol."

However, OpenAI says both models will still offer better usage efficiency than their predecessors, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

OpenAI is giving subscribers an extra usage reset

OpenAI says it won't charge users for the usage difference caused by the mistake, but it is offering something in return for the disruption.

"As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we'll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business," Sottiaux said.

I can confirm that a new reset has been added to ChatGPT, and it expires a month later. So, if you go to ChatGPT Settings > Usage and click Reset, you can restore your exhausted usage limits.

As much as I appreciate OpenAI giving its users a free usage reset, it's important to understand that this isn't equivalent to getting 40% less usage.

You're still going to use your tokens much faster, and it's unclear when OpenAI will reduce the costs.

It is worth noting that the change affects GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage, while other models retain their existing usage calculations.

Title: Drupal Warns of New Critical Flaw Exploited in the Wild
Context: Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites
Full Text:
Drupal fixes a critical flaw exploited in the wild that could let attackers take over vulnerable websites.

Drupal has warned of a new highly critical vulnerability in Drupal Core that attackers are actively exploiting to take over vulnerable websites.

Tracked as CVE-2026-136716, the flaw is related to improper handling of unusual or incomplete installation states. It is connected to CVE-2026-132165, also known as Fail2Install, which Drupal patched on November 18. However, the previous fix did not address every vulnerable installation scenario.

“SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites. It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.” Drupal maintainers warned.

The issue affects websites where the Drupal installer (install.php) remains remotely accessible. Drupal stressed that the vulnerability does not affect sites where administrators have already properly secured the installer.

One particularly concerning aspect is that administrators cannot easily identify affected installations through the Drupal interface. Moreover, sites that have already been compromised may no longer appear to be in the vulnerable state.

Drupal confirmed that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and urged administrators to investigate possible compromises.

“This is being exploited in the wild. Any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.” continues the advisory.

Recommended actions include reviewing logs for unauthorized access and unexpected changes involving the main administrative account, known as user 1. Administrators should also verify that its email address is under their control and consider resetting its password.

The vulnerability has been addressed in the following releases:

Drupal 11.4.x: Update to 11.4.14

Drupal 11.3.x: Update to 11.3.23

Drupal 10.6.x: Update to 10.6.23

Drupal 11.0.x through 11.2.x and 10.5.x and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive security fixes.

After updating, administrators should run update.php to fix affected installation states and ensure that the installer is properly secured on all existing and new websites.

Drupal’s own usage statistics provide further evidence of the exposure. Data published on November 15, 2026, show that thousands of websites still report running Drupal 8.x and tens of thousands use Drupal 9.x, both unsupported branches. Although these figures cover only sites reporting their versions through Drupal’s update system, they highlight the persistence of outdated installations and the need for organizations to migrate to supported releases.

Title: New GeoServer RCE exploit chain seen in the wild two days after disclosure
Context: In August, a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available, and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered...
Full Text:
Attackers have begun probing a chain of five GeoServer vulnerabilities that enables unauthenticated remote code execution, just two days after the open source geospatial server project disclosed the flaws.

Security firm watchTowr, which operates a global network of honeypot servers, reported that it observed the probing activity in the early morning hours of Wednesday. Attackers from multiple IP addresses created stored queries on GeoServer instances, checked whether they were created, and deleted them immediately, a technique that confirms a server is vulnerable without delivering a malicious payload.

GeoServer is widely used by government agencies, utilities, and large organizations to publish maps and geospatial data, and it has become a recurring target for attackers. The full RCE chain was reported to the project in August by Jonah Burgess, a senior security researcher at Rapid7 who uses the online handle CryptoCat. The GeoServer project shipped fixes in October and early November but only disclosed the vulnerabilities and published advisories for them on Monday.

Chained together, the flaws allow an external unauthenticated attacker to bypass security restrictions, read stored secrets, forge an administrator authentication cookie, and ultimately execute code on the underlying host. They affect GeoServer versions 3.0.0 to 3.0.1, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 2.27.6 and earlier. Users are advised to upgrade to the fixed versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7 depending on which major release they use.

A five-flaw chain

According to Burgess’ technical write-up this week, one flaw (CVE-2026-129244) uses an overly long stored-query request to trigger a filesystem error that exposes the server’s data-directory path. A second flaw (CVE-2026-129243) allows attackers to call services with a slash in their names, such as x/WFS, bypassing access rules and letting unprivileged users create and delete stored queries, an action normally reserved for administrators.

A saved query can then read files from the server, returning the administrator’s password digest along with a cookie-signing key that ships with the default value “geoserver,” a bug tracked as CVE-2026-120705. That key can then be used to forge an administrator cookie (CVE-2026-129245), and a deserialization bug in the database-backed user service finally allows running code with the privileges of the GeoServer process (CVE-2026-129242).

Only the final step results in code execution, and only one of the five flaws, the predictable signing key, is rated as critical. Burgess also published a proof-of-concept exploit for the chain.

However, researchers from Eye Security independently found a shorter, three-flaw RCE chain that shares the file-read step but reaches code execution through a different bug tracked as CVE-2026-120704 that was also patched.

Eye Security used AI models to find the bugs, and the fact that different researchers found some of the same vulnerabilities (two researchers named McCaulay and Quikko are also credited on some of the flaws) highlights the fact that attackers could use AI to find the flaws as well, especially since patches can serve as blueprints for AI agents. In fact, Eye Security had to consider whether delaying disclosure after patches were released was worth the risk of malicious actors finding them independently in the meantime.

“We used AI to find these bugs, and a determined attacker with good models could do the same, especially with the official patch to diff against,” Niels Teusink, a security researcher at Eye Security, wrote this week. “That makes the gap between releasing a fix and publishing details riskier than it used to be.”

After the advisories were published, it took less than two days for attackers to start probing the flaws to identify vulnerable servers, likely in preparation for attacks. Over 3,000 GeoServer instances are currently exposed to the internet.

GeoServer keeps getting targeted

This is not the first time GeoServer has been targeted by attackers. In August, a zero-day SQL injection flaw was exploited before a patch was available, and in December 2025 the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) ordered US agencies to patch another GeoServer flaw under active exploitation.

Upgrading to a patched release resolves the entire chain, but the patches generate a new cookie-signing key that invalidates existing remember-me sessions. Clustered deployments must set a shared GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY so nodes sign cookies with the same key, and since the data directory might have been exposed, administrators should also change their passwords.

Where patching cannot happen immediately, GeoServer advises blocking requests whose service value contains a slash, removing the remember-me filter from the web filter chain, and checking the data directory’s wfs/query folders for stored queries not created by a legitimate user.

Title: CISA Issues Alert After Danfoss Reveals Critical Flaw in Fridge Controllers
Context: Supermarkets and other operators of industrial refrigeration units have been advised to take action to mitigate a critical new flaw for which there is currently no patch
Full Text:
Supermarkets and other operators of industrial refrigeration units have been advised to take action to mitigate a critical new flaw for which there is currently no patch.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an ICS advisory on November 24 about CVE-2026-129713, which has a CVSS score of 9.8 and requires no authentication to exploit.

It said: “A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges.”

Despite the criticality of the flaw, Danfoss confirmed in an advisory on November 20 that it would not be addressed immediately, but in “upcoming software version 5.5.x.”

Read more on Danfoss flaws: France: Internet-Exposed Danfoss Controllers Drop 71% After Cyber-Attack

Until a patch is issued, the guidance from Danfoss, also shared by CISA, is as follows:

Follow the instructions in the product manual and don’t expose devices directly to the internet or assign them public IP addresses

Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture

Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict mode, which provides enhanced security protections

Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access

Danfoss said it would be removing the option for customers to disable Strict mode.

Food Retailers Braced for More Attacks

Operational technology (OT) including refrigeration controllers made by Danfoss was targeted in two waves of attacks in recent weeks linked to Iranian state actors.

The first, on October 11-12, targeted mainly French supermarkets such as Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, Leclerc, and Super U. As many as 700 sites were hit, with hackers able to compromise controllers and turn up the temperature to spoil food and in some cases start fires.

Some reports cited figures of “tens of millions of euros” lost nationwide in a single day.

The second wave came on November 1-2 and used the same playbook, although this time retailers in at least 12 countries across Europe were affected. Blood banks in France were also reportedly hit.

In both campaigns, affected controllers included older Danfoss models that no longer received security updates (AK-SM800 and AK-SC355) and/or newer models running outdated firmware (AK-SM800A).

Retailers in the UK were largely unaffected as Danfoss is a less popular brand in the country. A major industry effort was launched to ensure that legacy flaws from a manufacturer called RDM were patched to improve cyber resilience in the sector, according to Pen Test Partners.

Title: Palo Alto confirms Fragnesia exploitation against firewalls in PHP2Shell attacks
Context: “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks has confirmed that attackers exploited Fragnesia, a Linux kernel flaw, to gain root on PAN-OS firewalls through the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, and has shipped fixes six months after the bug was patched in Linux.

The vulnerability allows a locally authenticated, low-privileged attacker to escalate privileges to root.

“Exploitation of CVE-2026-46300 has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet,” the company said in its November 25 security advisory. It added that all observed attacks targeted devices whose management interface “is exposed to the internet, a configuration our best practices advise against.”

Even so, the company labeled the bulletin “Informational” and gave it no CVSS score. Fixed builds span every supported PAN-OS branch from 10.2 to 12.2.

A second patch cycle in a month

For PAN-OS customers, these are the second set of hotfixes in a month. Between October 25 and October 29, Palo Alto released fixes for PHP2Shell, according to the timeline in its PHP2Shell advisory. PHP2Shell is the collective name for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two critical flaws in the PHP runtime behind the PAN-OS management web interface.

The company rated both flaws 9.2 on CVSS 4.0, and the advisory, which covers PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama, said, “active exploitation has been observed.”

The October builds do not include the kernel fix, which arrives in later releases listed in the new bulletin. Even for customers who have patched PHP2Shell, Palo Alto said in the bulletin that it “still recommend[s] upgrading to a fixed release at your next maintenance interval.”

Palo Alto is relaxed about the timing. “If you are running a fixed PAN-OS listed in the CVE-2026-109618 advisory, you are protected,” the bulletin said. “The only known way to exploit this vulnerability requires an attacker to first exploit the PHP2Shell vulnerability,” it added. For devices with management access restricted to trusted internal IP addresses, it advises upgrading “at your next maintenance interval.”

Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said that the approach is defensible when vulnerabilities are chained.

“It’s acceptable to apply one patch that effectively breaks the chain. Ideally, all vulnerabilities would be patched as early as possible, but in many cases this is not practical,” Brown said.

Rahul Karne, a senior digital forensics and incident response analyst, called patching PHP2Shell a reasonable short-term step, but said it blocks the known way in without fixing the bug.

“The key word is ‘known,’” Karne said. He pointed out that public exploit code for Fragnesia, including a Metasploit module, is available, and that any other code execution flaw on the device would make the kernel bug usable again.

From web shell to root

The chain has been public for almost a month. In late October, Dream Security researchers reported that attackers combined PHP2Shell with Fragnesia to compromise firewalls running vulnerable PAN-OS builds.

According to Dream, the attackers used PHP2Shell to run code as the web service account and then used the kernel flaw to become root. From there, they tunneled into internal networks and stole credentials, private keys, and network topology data.

The kernel bug itself is not new. William Bowling, a researcher at Zellic, disclosed Fragnesia on May 13 along with a proof-of-concept exploit and an upstream kernel patch, after finding it with the help of the company’s V12 AI auditing agent. Fedora shipped a fixed kernel the next day.

Karne said some delay is normal for appliance vendors that maintain custom kernels across many hardware models, but 195 days is too long when exploit code is public. Customers should hear whether they are affected within a week of such a disclosure and get a fix within about 30 days, he said.

“A firewall should not get security fixes more slowly than the servers it protects,” Karne said.

The firewall as a foothold

Palo Alto is not the only security vendor whose appliances were rooted this way. In November, Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers were hit after attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Gaia OS privilege escalation flaw to take over gateways and deploy a wiper.

Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said CISOs should treat the incident as a weakness in their trust model for security appliances, not merely a patching issue.

“A firewall running Linux, PHP and other third-party components must be assessed with the same rigor as any privileged, internet-facing server,” Daftary said. “Vendor labels such as ‘Informational’ should never override enterprise risk analysis when flaws can be chained to achieve root access.”

“If a device is exposed during the attack window, merely applying the hotfix does not establish trust,” she added. Teams should review administrative access, rotate credentials and certificates, hunt for persistence, and reimage the appliance from a known-good build when root compromise cannot be ruled out, she said. Asked why the kernel fix took six months to reach PAN-OS, and whether Panorama is affected, Palo Alto said it had “no further information to share beyond what is outlined in the advisory at this time.”

Title: Critical Juniper Session Smart Conductor Flaw Exploited in Attacks
Context: Juniper Networks and the US cybersecurity agency CISA this week warned that threat actors have been exploiting a critical vulnerability in Session Smart Conductor
Full Text:
Juniper Networks and the US cybersecurity agency CISA this week warned that threat actors have been exploiting a critical vulnerability in Session Smart Conductor.

Tracked as CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score of 9.8), the security defect is described as a remotely exploitable OS command injection bug.

It affects the Session Smart Conductor’s AutomatedProvisioner service and could allow attackers to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges via a specially crafted Salt minion ID.

A centralized management and policy solution, Session Smart Conductor is used for the orchestration and management of Session Smart Routers across networks. The Salt minion ID is a router’s unique ID when registering with the Salt master (Session Smart Conductor).

CVE-2026-103406 was patched on October 28 along with 17 other flaws in Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor. On Tuesday, Juniper updated its advisory to flag the security defect as exploited.

“At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT. Customers are encouraged to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime take steps to mitigate this vulnerability,” reads Juniper’s update.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

On Wednesday, CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days, as mandated by BOD 26-04.

Although BOD 26-04 only applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies, all organizations are advised to review CISA’s KEV list and address the relevant security weaknesses as soon as possible.

Juniper patched CVE-2026-103406 in Session Smart Router and Session Smart Conductor versions 7.2.3, 7.1.7, and 7.0.5.

CISA also added five Mitel MiCollab flaws, a Vates Xen Orchestra issue, and three Danfoss AK-SM 800A series vulnerabilities to the KEV list.

Title: Mitel MiCollab Zero-Days Exploited in Suspected AI-Assisted Attacks
Context: Threat actors exploited several Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities as zero-days in a data theft campaign, according to Accenture’s Apex Labs
Full Text:
Threat actors exploited several Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities as zero-days in a data theft campaign, according to Accenture’s Apex Labs. CISA on Wednesday added five MiCollab flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

In one attack observed by Accenture, hackers gained privileged access to a MiCollab server and quickly reached the targeted organization’s identity infrastructure, ultimately stealing sensitive business information.

The MiCollab business collaboration platform enables employees to communicate through calls, messages, and virtual meetings. Accenture noted that the product’s frequent internet exposure and integration with Active Directory make it particularly attractive to hackers.

Mitel on November 16 announced patches for five vulnerabilities affecting the product’s audio, web and video conferencing component, including arbitrary file upload, XML injection, unauthorized access, command injection, and authentication bypass. They can all be exploited by unauthenticated attackers, and two critical bugs allow arbitrary command execution.

The security holes are tracked as CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133311, CVE-2026-133323, and CVE-2026-133324.

Accenture found evidence that the vulnerabilities were exploited in the wild before Mitel published its advisory. The company determined that threat actors deployed a web shell on a victim’s systems on November 15.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Accenture, the attackers executed commands on a MiCollab server just 12 minutes after the first request, and gained root privileges within half an hour.

The hackers harvested additional credentials and, roughly 20 hours after their first observed request, gained access to internal backup and database servers.

The investigation uncovered evidence that some of the malicious activity may have been driven by AI tools, with the attacker’s infrastructure communicating with two unnamed commercial AI API services.

“Because the telemetry is sampled, Apex Labs cannot determine precisely how the threat actor used the services. However, the observed activity is consistent with potential uses such as data triage, operational support for exploitation or web-shell activity, and preparation of extortion material,” Accenture noted.

It added that communications between the attackers’ infrastructure and the AI services resumed — after an eight-hour silence — at precisely the same second that the hackers sent an authentication bypass request to the targeted MiCollab server.

The company also found evidence of compromise at a second victim, with a MiCollab server communicating with the same attacker’s infrastructure since November 9. However, Accenture could not establish how the second server was hacked, as it had been affected by older vulnerabilities as well.

The researchers have not linked the attacks to a known cybercrime group, but believe they may have been part of an extortion campaign.

Mitel has released patches, but its advisory — last updated on November 24 — does not mention in-the-wild exploitation of the vulnerabilities.

Accenture warned organizations that attackers may have compromised their MiCollab servers before the fixes were installed and urged them to check for indicators of compromise (IoCs).

CISA added all five vulnerabilities to its KEV catalog, instructing federal agencies to address four of them by November 28; the last one has a December 9 deadline.

Threat actors regularly target Mitel products. CISA’s KEV catalog currently includes a dozen such vulnerabilities.

Title: Drupal Installer Patch Left a Gap Attackers Are Already Exploiting
Context: Drupal says last week’s patch for an exploited installer vulnerability did not protect every website, and attackers are now leveraging the gap to hack vulnerable sites
Full Text:
Drupal says last week’s patch for an exploited installer vulnerability did not protect every website, and attackers are now leveraging the gap to hack vulnerable sites.

The new issue, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 with a CMSS score of 21/25, was disclosed on November 25, exactly a week after Drupal announced the original patch in advisory SA-CORE-2026-017. Drupal describes the new flaw as an access bypass issue that can lead to site takeover.

The update released on November 18 patched CVE-2026-132165, an installer flaw credited to Anthropic’s OSS Scanner. The affected installer ships with Drupal core and enables users to set up a new site.

Drupal was informed of in-the-wild exploitation soon after, and CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV catalog on November 24.

The advisory for CVE-2026-136716 explains where the earlier fix fell short.

“SA-CORE-2026-017 recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer. However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites,” Drupal said in its advisory.

It added, “It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state.”

Drupal warned that CVE-2026-136716 is being exploited in the wild and “any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.”

Websites where the installer had already been secured are not vulnerable to attacks. Patches are included in versions 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23. Affected production sites must run an update hook after upgrading to fully address the vulnerability.

Drupal has not shared any information on the attacks, and it’s unclear who is responsible for the exploitation. Users have been advised to check logs for signs of compromise.

Title: Drupal Warns of New Highly Critical Site Takeover Vulnerability Under Active Exploitation
Context: Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild
Full Text:
Drupal has warned of a new "highly critical" security flaw impacting Drupal core that it said has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-136716 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a case of improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions. It also relates to CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install in that it addresses remaining vulnerable installation states that could still be abused to facilitate site takeover even after the fix.

CVE-2026-132165 "recently fixed several vulnerabilities within the Drupal core installer," Drupal maintainers said. "However, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover following that advisory, including production sites."

"It is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state, and sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state."

Drupal acknowledged that the vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, but emphasized that site owners who have already secured the installer ("install.php") are not impacted.

Specifically, any website that left its installer remotely accessible following the fix for CVE-2026-132165 may have been compromised. Drupal is urging site administrators to take the following actions -

Check site logs for unauthorized access, including unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account

Ensure the user 1 email address is set to under their control, and consider resetting user 1's password.

The issue has been remediated in the following versions -

Drupal 11.4.x - Update to Drupal 11.4.14

Drupal 11.3.x - Update to Drupal 11.3.23

Drupal 10.6.x - Update to Drupal 10.6.23

Drupal 11.0.x to 11.2.x - No fix (End-of-life)

Drupal 10.5.x and below - No fix (End-of-life)

After updating to the latest supported versions, it's recommended to run "update.php" to fix existing production sites in this state and secure the Drupal installer on all new and existing sites.

According to statistics shared by StepSecurity, there are about 55,800 internet-facing Drupal sites as of November 26, 2026, out of which 31,500 services are running branches that are vulnerable to CVE-2026-132165 and roughly 15,000 are on the end-of-life 8 and 9 branches.

Title: Hackers Exploit 10 Vulnerabilities Across Mitel, Juniper, Vates, and Danfoss Products
Context: Evidence indicates the deployment of a web shell against one victim organization a day before Mitel released patches, only for the intrusion to progress rapidly and allowing the...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added 10 security flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including five vulnerabilities impacting Mitel MiCollab that were disclosed last week.

The Mitel MiCollab vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An arbitrary file upload vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to upload arbitrary files to the target system.

CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score: 9.0) - An XML injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score: 5.9) - An unauthorized access vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information.

CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A command injection vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system.

CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An authentication bypass vulnerability in the Audio, Web, and Video Conferencing (AWV) Component of MiCollab that could allow an attacker to bypass authentication controls and perform unauthorized actions within the context of the application.

The issues affect MiCollab versions 10.3 and earlier. "Mitel provided a patch available for release 10.3 (10.3.0.18) that addresses these vulnerabilities," the company said in an advisory published November 16, 2026. "Upgrade to this release and apply the provided patch, or upgrade to a later release."

Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. As of writing, there are currently no details on how the vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild.

Customers who are unable to apply the updates are recommended to mitigate the risk by restricting external access to the AWV component. The addition comes against the backdrop of a report from Accenture's Apex Labs, which revealed that an unknown threat actor may have been weaponizing the flaws as zero-days as part of what's suspected to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted data theft campaign.

Evidence indicates the deployment of a web shell against one victim organization a day before Mitel released patches, only for the intrusion to progress rapidly and allowing the threat actor to harvest credentials and steal sensitive business data from a line-of-business database server within hours.

"At that victim, we found the threat actor ran its first command 12 minutes after its first request, then reached root on the MiCollab server within 30 minutes and used the directory credentials that MiCollab stores for its LDAP connector to authenticate to a domain controller within 32 minutes," Accenture said.

The activity is assessed to be part of a broader campaign targeting MiCollab instances, with a second organization's MiCollab server observed holding a persistent HTTPS channel to the threat actor infrastructure since November 9, 2026. It has not been established how this server was compromised as it had been found running an older MiCollab version affected by previously disclosed flaws (i.e., MTLVULN-1694).

The indicators of compromise associated with the intrusions are listed below -

204.76.203[.]204 (Command-and-control server)

204.76.203[.]216

204.76-203-204.sslip[.]io

204.76.203[.]204/bkup/ (Data exfiltration path)

204.76.203[.]204/bkdl/ (Tool download path)

"MiCollab presents an attractive target because it is commonly internet-facing and connected to critical enterprise services, including Active Directory," Accenture said. "Its history of exploitation further underscores this risk."

Also added to the KEV catalog are the following vulnerabilities -

CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper validation of specified type of input vulnerability in Vates Xen Orchestra that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and perform actions with administrative privileges via a specially crafted authentication token containing an empty JSON object.

CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root via a specially crafted salt minion ID.

The addition of CVE-2026-133469 follows an advisory from Vates VMS that the vulnerability, also tracked as VSA-2026-062, has been exploited by a threat actor from the following IP address and TOR domain -

91.211.251[.]112:8001

ustar3rqxgnskzgnwkgpofgtvxevm6cx3lxdbwt4mndtveqyaohid[.]onion:3333

"At least one instance of malicious exploitation of CVE-2026-103406 has been reported to the Juniper SIRT," Juniper Networks said in an advisory. "Customers are encouraged to upgrade to a fixed release as soon as possible and in the meantime take steps to mitigate this vulnerability."

The remaining three security flaws relate to Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series refrigeration controllers that could lead to authentication bypass and arbitrary command execution -

CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A path traversal vulnerability that could allow an attacker to access and read underlying server system files via the XML interface.

CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to run arbitrary commands on the affected system.

CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score: 8.5) - An improper authentication vulnerability that could allow an attacker to generate a web report exposing sensitive information, including internal IP addresses, usernames, and store names.

Although Danfoss makes no mention of the flaws being exploited, it's likely that they were put to use as part of high-impact attacks targeting supermarket chains across Europe in recent weeks. France has attributed the October 2026 attacks on its retail sites to Shahid Kaveh (aka Cyber Aveng3rs and Cyber Isnaad Front), an Iranian cyber unit affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are being advised to apply the necessary fixes for all the flaws, except CVE-2026-133311 and CVE-2025-41450, by November 28, 2026. The remaining two vulnerabilities must be addressed by December 9, 2026.

CISA Warns of New Unpatched Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series Flaw

The development comes as CISA has warned of an unpatched critical flaw in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series (CVE-2026-129713, CVSS score: 9.8 / 9.3) controllers that could be exploited to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges.

"A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges," CISA said. "Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability."

Danfoss, which has issued an alert of its own, said the security flaw impacts versions 5.4.0 and earlier. A fix for the vulnerability is expected to be addressed in an upcoming software version (5.5.x). It also said it will remove the option that allows customers to disable "Strict mode" in the product.

Until the fixes are available, system administrators are advised to take the following actions -

Make sure remote access to the units is possible only through a secure VPN or in general over a protected network

Configure the units to Strict mode, which ensures higher security levels on the product

Recommend using strong passwords

CISA is also recommending that organizations minimize network exposure of such devices, place control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls, and isolate them from business networks.

"When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available," CISA added. "Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices."

Title: U.S. CISA adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability...
Full Text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the following HPE, Danfoss, Mitel MiCollab, and Vates Xen Orchestra flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability

CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability

CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability

The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25914 (CVSS score of 7.5), is a path traversal vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration management systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit improper restrictions on file paths to retrieve and read files from the underlying system through the XML interface. Access to sensitive files could provide information useful for further compromising the device. There are no publicly confirmed reports of exploitation in the wild or threat actors associated with this vulnerability. Danfoss addressed the issue in software version 3.3.

The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2023-25915 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical improper input validation vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 800A systems running software versions prior to 3.3. An authenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient input validation to execute arbitrary commands on the target system, potentially gaining full control of the affected refrigeration controller. Despite its critical severity and the potential consequences for operational technology environments, there are no publicly confirmed reports linking this specific vulnerability to attacks in the wild or identifying threat actors exploiting it. Danfoss released software version 3.3 to address the issue.

The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-41450 (CVSS score of 8.2), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series systems running software versions prior to 4.2. The authentication bypass allows an attacker to generate web reports without proper authorization, potentially exposing sensitive information such as internal IP addresses, usernames and store names. The vulnerability was identified by researchers at Claroty’s Team82. Although it affects the same family of refrigeration controllers targeted in the European supermarket attacks, there is no public confirmation that attackers exploited this particular CVE during those incidents. Danfoss addressed the vulnerability in software version 4.2.

The fourth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-103406 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting HPE Juniper Session Smart Conductor. The flaw resides in the AutomatedProvisioner component and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges by supplying a specially crafted Salt minion ID. The vulnerability has been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming exploitation in the wild. However, no specific threat actor or ransomware campaign has been publicly attributed to these attacks. Administrators should apply the security updates provided by Juniper, including versions 7.0.5, 7.1.7 and 7.2.3 for the affected release branches.

The fifth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133275 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an unrestricted file upload vulnerability affecting the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component of Mitel MiCollab. The vulnerability affects MiCollab version 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient file type validation to upload arbitrary files to the target system. Depending on the nature of the uploaded files and the system configuration, this could provide an opportunity for further malicious activity. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified any threat actors associated with this vulnerability. The company released a security patch for affected installations.

The sixth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133303 (CVSS score of 9.0), is a critical XML injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter validation and leverage malicious content staged in advance to perform XML injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the system. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the affected installation. Mitel has not disclosed any confirmed exploitation in the wild or identified threat actors behind attacks exploiting this flaw. A security patch is available for affected MiCollab installations.

The seventh flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133311 (CVSS score of 5.9), is an improper authentication vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knows a specific system-generated random identifier or has access to malicious content staged in advance could exploit the weakness to obtain sensitive information. The vulnerability is limited to the affected functionality and does not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary files elsewhere on the system. No confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been publicly reported. Mitel has released a security patch to address the issue.

The eighth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133323 (CVSS score of 10.0), is a critical OS command injection vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient parameter sanitization to perform blind command injection and execute arbitrary commands within the context of the affected system. Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity and availability. Mitel has not reported confirmed exploitation in the wild or attributed attacks to specific threat actors. A security patch is available to address the vulnerability.

The ninth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133324 (CVSS score of 5.3), is an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting the AWV component of Mitel MiCollab. Improper handling of authentication could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass security controls and perform unauthorized actions within the application. Successful exploitation could compromise the security of the affected installation. No publicly confirmed exploitation or associated threat actors have been reported. Mitel has released a security patch for the affected versions.

The tenth flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-133469 (CVSS score of 9.8), is a critical authentication bypass vulnerability affecting Vates Xen Orchestra, a management and backup platform for XCP-ng and XenServer environments. The vulnerability affects versions prior to 6.9.2 and 6.10.1. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of authentication tokens by supplying a specially crafted cookie containing an empty JSON object. The application may then authenticate the attacker as the owner of an existing, unexpired token. Once authenticated, the attacker could retrieve reusable authentication token identifiers, potentially enabling persistent unauthorized access to the environment. The vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild, although no specific threat actors have been publicly identified. Vates addressed the issue in Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.2 and 6.10.1.

The Danfoss vulnerabilities deserve particular attention because they affect the same family of refrigeration management systems involved in the cyberattacks targeting European supermarkets in October and November 2026.

The first wave of attacks, detected between October 11 and 12, compromised refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail sites in France. Attackers manipulated defrost settings, forcing refrigeration equipment to operate at excessively high temperatures. The incidents resulted in substantial food losses and at least 15 reported fires. A second wave between November 1 and 2 affected retailers across several other European countries.

The French authorities’ investigation attributed the October attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit associated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). However, responsibility for the subsequent November attacks across Europe has not been conclusively established.

The technical evidence points to the exploitation of internet-exposed refrigeration management interfaces, with default credentials and outdated firmware considered likely entry points. However, investigators have not confirmed that CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915 or CVE-2025-41450 were specifically exploited during these operations. The incidents instead highlight the risks associated with exposing operational technology (OT) systems directly to the internet without adequate authentication, network segmentation and security updates.

An additional development is worth mentioning: a November 2026 advisory from Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre reported research by Midnight Blue identifying six previously unknown pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, affecting firmware versions up to and including 5.3.2. At the time of the advisory, these flaws had not yet received CVE identifiers and no patches were available. Researchers also warned that attackers could establish persistence surviving factory resets and firmware updates. These findings add another layer of concern to the security of refrigeration infrastructure. ncsc.gov.ie

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA order U.S. federal civilian agencies to remediate eight of them by November 28, 2026, and the remaining two by December 9, 2026. The individual deadlines are:

November 28, 2026: CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2026-103406, CVE-2026-133275, CVE-2026-133303, CVE-2026-133323, CVE-2026-133324 and CVE-2026-133469.

December 9, 2026: CVE-2025-41450 and CVE-2026-133311.

Title: Risky Biz Podcast: Eliminating Vulnerabilities Without Upgrading Dependencies
Context: Meanwhile, attackers are exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities faster than organizations can respond
Full Text:
Risky Biz Podcast: Eliminating Vulnerabilities Without Upgrading Dependencies

Security teams are often responsible for remediating vulnerabilities in applications that no longer have engineering resources assigned to them. Even a minor dependency upgrade can introduce performance regressions, break production services, or require extensive regression testing. Meanwhile, attackers are exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities faster than organizations can respond.

In a new Risky Business sponsor interview, Socket founder and CEO Feross Aboukhadijeh joins James to discuss Socket's ambition to eliminate every patchable open source vulnerability and how advances in AI are making that possible at scale.

The conversation explores how Socket delivers security fixes for the exact dependency versions organizations already run, without requiring upgrades or introducing breaking API changes.

James presses Feross on some of the harder technical questions behind this approach:

How do you safely backport a security fix across multiple generations of a package?

How can testing the thousands of packages that depend on a vulnerable library help validate a fix?

Can AI make comprehensive CVE remediation economically feasible?

How does Socket prevent the delivery of security fixes from becoming another supply chain attack vector?

Feross also discusses why Socket makes its fixes for critical vulnerabilities freely available to the open source community and what it could take to remediate vulnerabilities in live production applications without redeploying them.
